uncited: The dataset is analyzed to build a data structure that maps spatial locations or value ranges to the cells within the volume.
For a given isovalue $q$, the search structure is queried to enumerate only the "active" cells $c$ where the isosurface might exist.
Multiple isosurfaces or isovalue queries are performed on the same static dataset.
The dataset is large enough that skipping non-active cells saves more time than the index lookup overhead.

See [Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction](1230-standard-interval-tree-for-isosurface-extraction.md) and [Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction](1252-fixed-sized-buckets-for-isosurface-extraction.md).

detail: supported

Search Data Structure Based Isosurface Extraction is a family of methods that utilize external search structures (indices) to accelerate isosurface extraction for multiple queries on the same dataset [S1].

The claim states that 'Search Data Structure Based Isosurface Extraction' is a family of methods using external search structures to accelerate isosurface extraction for multiple queries on the same dataset. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3, stating: 'the use of external search structures allows speeding up the isosurface extraction process when multiple queries are performed on the same dataset.' It further classifies these methods into range-based, domain-based, and contour propagation techniques, all of which utilize indices (kd-trees, interval trees, octrees) to disregard non-active cells, thereby supporting the definition provided in the claim.
supported
The spatial domain of the dataset is hierarchically partitioned to disregard parts of the volume that do not contain active cells for a given isovalue [S1].

The claim states that the spatial domain is hierarchically partitioned to disregard parts of the volume that do not contain active cells for a given isovalue. Source [S1] explicitly states under 'Domain-based' techniques: 'the domain spanned by the dataset is hierarchically partitioned to disregard the parts of the volume not containing active cells.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
This approach was investigated to achieve high performance levels in isosurface extraction, particularly in the context of parallelization and distributed environments [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the authors investigated possible parallelization strategies of the Marching Cubes algorithm to achieve high performance levels. It further details various approaches (search structures, contour propagation) used in the context of isosurface extraction. While the evidence notes limitations for single-use or transfer-heavy scenarios, it confirms that these approaches were indeed investigated for performance optimization, including parallelization.
supported

This approach is distinct from single-pass methods because the overhead of index construction must be amortized over multiple queries; it is not feasible if the dataset is examined only once or if the index transfer overhead is prohibitive [S1].

The claim states that the approach is distinct from single-pass methods because index construction overhead must be amortized over multiple queries, and it is not feasible if the dataset is examined only once or if index transfer overhead is prohibitive. Source [S1] explicitly supports this by stating that search structures speed up extraction for 'multiple queries' and are not feasible if 'a dataset is examined only once' (because index creation time plus extraction time exceeds simple traversal) or if 'a dataset needs to be transferred for the analysis on a different resource' (due to download overhead).
supported
The core principle of this family is the pre-computation of a spatial or value-based index to filter out inactive cells during the query phase [S1].

The claim states that the core principle involves pre-computing a spatial or value-based index to filter out inactive cells during the query phase. The evidence explicitly describes 'APPROACHES BASED ON SEARCH DATA STRUCTURES' where an index is created to 'disregard large regions containing... only non-active cells.' It further details 'Range-based' techniques (value-based, using kd-trees/interval trees) and 'Domain-based' techniques (spatial, using octrees) which fit the description of pre-computed indices used to filter inactive cells.
supported

By creating an index that allows the algorithm to disregard regions containing only non-active cells, these methods achieve significant performance gains over brute-force traversal when repeated queries are required [S1].

The claim states that creating an index allows the algorithm to disregard regions with only non-active cells, leading to performance gains for repeated queries. The evidence explicitly states: 'the use of external search structures allows speeding up the isosurface extraction process when multiple queries are performed on the same dataset. This result is achieved by creating an index on the data that permits to disregard large regions containing, for a given isovalue, only non-active cells.' This directly supports every part of the claim.
supported
The isosurface is traced via breadth-first traversal through face-adjacencies starting from the seed cells corresponding to the required isovalue [S1].

The claim states that the isosurface is traced via breadth-first traversal through face-adjacencies starting from seed cells corresponding to the required isovalue. Source [S1] explicitly states under the 'Contour propagation' section: 'The isosurface can be traced by a breadth-first traversal through the face-adjacencies, starting from the cells of the seed sets corresponding to the required isovalue'. This matches the claim exactly.
supported

The total execution time is the sum of index creation time and extraction time [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that for a dataset examined only once, 'the time necessary to create any of these indices plus the execution of the isosurface extraction is normally greater than the traversal of all the cells.' This phrasing treats the total time as the sum of index creation time and extraction time, thereby supporting the claim.

Cells that are definitively inactive (where $q$ falls outside the cell's value range or spatial bounds) are skipped [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that search structures allow the process to 'disregard large regions containing... only non-active cells' and that domain-based techniques partition the domain to 'disregard the parts of the volume not containing active cells.' This aligns with the claim that inactive cells (those outside the relevant value range or spatial bounds) are skipped/disregarded.

Cells (or fixed-size groups of cells) are associated with a continuous value range $R(c) = [\min_{p \in C} f(p), \max_{p \in C} f(p)]$, where $f(p)$ is the scalar field value at vertex $p$ [S1].

The claim states that cells (or fixed-size groups of cells) are associated with a continuous value range $R(c) = [min_{p∈C} f(p), max_{p∈C} f(p)]$. This is explicitly stated in Source [S1] under the 'Range-based' section: 'each cell c (or group of cells with a fixed size) is associated with the continuous set of values considering the lowest and the greatest value taken on by the function over its vertices: R(c) = [minp∈C f (p), maxp∈C f (p)].' The notation and definition match exactly.
supported
A query for isovalue $q$ enumerates all cells $c$ such that $q \in R(c)$ [S1].

The claim states that a query for isovalue $q$ enumerates all cells $c$ such that $q ∈ R(c)$. Source [S1] explicitly states under the 'Range-based' section: 'The isosurface extraction query concerns the enumeration of all cells c such as the isovalue q ∈ R(c).' Additionally, the notes define $R(c)$ as the range of values for cell $c$. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
